title: Grafana unified alerting -- multi-dimensional rules and notification policies
exp: Grafana's alerting engine (unified alerting, the modern default since v9) evaluates queries on a schedule and routes firing alerts through a policy tree to notification channels. For a 50-source pipeline, one well-designed rule replaces 50 manually created alarms.
pts: An alert rule = a query (usually the same CloudWatch query type from Day 10) + a condition (threshold) + an evaluation interval + a 'for' duration the condition must hold before firing.

Multi-dimensional alerting: if your query returns multiple series (one per Source dimension value), Grafana creates a SEPARATE alert instance per series automatically -- one rule definition, many independent alert instances, each labeled by its dimension value.

Alert states: Normal -> Pending (condition true, waiting out the 'for' duration) -> Alerting (notification sent) -> Normal again once resolved. Pending prevents single noisy spikes from paging someone.

Notification policies form a tree matched by label: a default policy catches everything, more specific policies match on labels (like source=Bloomberg) and can route to a different contact point or add a delay.
Contact points: Slack webhook, email, PagerDuty, generic webhook -- configured once, reused across many notification policies.
Mute timings suppress notifications during known maintenance windows without disabling the underlying alert rule.

The classic pipeline alert set: 'no records processed in the last 25 hours' (per source, catches silent failures), 'error rate > 5%' (per source, data quality), 'EMR cluster idle > 30 min' (cost), 'job duration > 2x rolling average' (performance regression).
pr: Design the alert rule set for the 50-source pipeline: list each rule, its threshold, its for duration, and its severity label

viz.cap: One rule definition fans out into per-source alert instances, then routes by label

qa.q: How does one Grafana alert rule generate 50 separate alerts for 50 sources?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** When the underlying query returns multiple time series (because the CloudWatch dimension wasn't pinned to a single value), Grafana automatically creates one independent alert instance per series, each carrying that series' label (Source=Bloomberg, Source=ICE, etc.). Each instance evaluates and fires independently -- Bloomberg going silent doesn't affect ICE's alert state. You write and maintain one rule, not fifty.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** T-SQL engine parses, compiles into execution plans, caches them in the plan cache, and executes via the storage engine (buffer pool & latching).

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Parameter sniffing and missing stats cause sub-optimal plan compilation, resulting in full table scans and high CPU.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Parameterization improves plan reuse, but recompile hints (OPTION RECOMPILE) may be needed for skewed data distributions.

qa.q: What is the purpose of the for duration on an alert rule, and when would you set it to zero?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** For requires the condition to remain true for that entire duration before the alert transitions from Pending to actually firing -- it filters out single noisy spikes. Set it to a real duration (like 10m) for noisy/bursty metrics. Set it to 0 when the condition already represents a meaningfully delayed signal -- 'zero records in the last 25 hours' is already checking a full day-plus window, so no additional spike-filtering is needed.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Signals build a fine-grained reactive dependency graph. When a signal value changes, only dependent view nodes are scheduled for DOM updating.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Mutating signal values inside effects without untracked() causes infinite change detection loops and browser freeze.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Signals provide predictable synchronous reactivity without Zone.js overhead, but require adapting existing RxJS-heavy codebases.

qa.q: What is a notification policy tree and why not just attach a contact point directly to each alert rule?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** The policy tree matches alerts to contact points based on labels, independent of the alert rule definition -- so you can change routing (Bloomberg-source alerts to a specific Slack channel, critical-severity to PagerDuty) without touching any alert rule. New rules automatically get correctly routed as long as they carry the right labels, without editing the rule itself.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Cloud control plane APIs orchestrate virtualized hardware, networking (VPC/VNets), IAM policies, and auto-scaling groups.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Overly permissive IAM roles (wildcard actions) or unmonitored resource limits lead to security breaches and unexpected cloud cost spikes.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Serverless/managed services eliminate infrastructure maintenance but introduce cold starts and vendor lock-in.

qa.q: What is a mute timing and how is it different from disabling an alert rule?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** A mute timing suppresses notifications during a defined window (e.g. a maintenance window) while the rule keeps evaluating and its state history keeps recording normally -- you just don't get paged. Disabling the rule stops evaluation entirely, losing the record of whether the condition was true during that window. Mute timings suit planned downtime; disabling suits a rule you're actively reworking.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Cloud control plane APIs orchestrate virtualized hardware, networking (VPC/VNets), IAM policies, and auto-scaling groups.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Overly permissive IAM roles (wildcard actions) or unmonitored resource limits lead to security breaches and unexpected cloud cost spikes.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Serverless/managed services eliminate infrastructure maintenance but introduce cold starts and vendor lock-in.
